passages.title: The first census
passages.summary: God commands a census of men eligible for war. Tribal leaders assist Moses and Aaron. Levites receive separate duties.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How do the camp's different duties help people support each other?

contextNote.title: The census counts a defined task rather than the whole population
contextNote.text: The count focuses on men old enough to serve in war. It therefore does not list every person living in the camp. Tribal leaders organize the count, while Levites receive separate responsibilities. These totals prepare the account for movement and conflict.

passages.title: The camp arranged
passages.summary: The tribes camp around the meeting tent in four groups. Their marching order follows the same arrangement.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider what your daily arrangements show about your priorities.

contextNote.title: The arrangement makes the sanctuary a shared center
contextNote.text: The tribes receive places around the meeting tent rather than independent camps without relation. Their marching order preserves that larger arrangement during movement. The center carries sacred duties instead of belonging to one tribe's army. Space becomes a way to describe both common identity and distinct responsibilities.

passages.title: Levites and firstborn
passages.summary: The chapter names Aaron’s sons and assigns duties to the Levite families. Levites stand in place of Israel’s firstborn.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects the firstborn with Israel's escape from Egypt.

contextNote.title: Levite service recalls a claim arising from the rescue
contextNote.text: God describes taking the Levites in place of Israel's firstborn sons. This explanation joins present duties with the earlier departure from Egypt. The counting and redemption payments organize that substitution in practical terms. A rescued people carries obligations that reach beyond remembering the rescue in words.

passages.title: Duties for moving the sanctuary
passages.summary: Moses and Aaron count Levites assigned to service. Kohath, Gershon, and Merari have different transport duties.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how careful preparation can help others carry their responsibilities.

contextNote.title: Moving sacred objects requires divisions of responsibility
contextNote.text: Priests cover the furnishings before others carry them. The carriers must follow limits on touching and seeing the objects. Different families transport different parts of the dwelling. The account makes coordinated work necessary for keeping a sacred center within a traveling camp.

passages.title: Camp, restitution, and jealousy
passages.summary: The laws cover camp rules and repayment for wrongs. They include a ceremony for accusations against a wife.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What power does a husband's accusation give him? What protection does the wife receive?

contextNote.title: Suspicion enters a ritual with unequal household power
contextNote.text: The procedure begins with a husband's jealousy, including suspicion without witnesses. It places the accused wife within a public priestly rite. The chapter supplies no matching procedure for a wife suspecting her husband. Its appeal to divine judgment does not erase that unequal starting position.

passages.title: Nazirite vows and blessing
passages.summary: People can make a special vow to God. It limits wine, hair cutting, and contact with the dead. God also gives priests words of blessing.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how a commitment can shape daily conduct. Read the blessing as a prayer for God’s care.

contextNote.title: A special vow creates duties for a stated period
contextNote.text: Women and men can enter the dedication described here. The restrictions govern drink, hair, and contact with death while the vow lasts. An unexpected death nearby requires beginning the dedicated period again. The chapter then moves from individual vows to words blessing the whole people.

passages.title: Gifts from the tribal leaders
passages.summary: Tribal leaders bring wagons, oxen, and offerings for the sanctuary. Each leader’s altar gift receives a separate account.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how material gifts and practical support can make shared worship possible.

contextNote.title: The same gift does not answer every form of work
contextNote.text: Wagons and oxen go to Levite families according to their transport tasks. The Kohathites receive none because they carry sacred furnishings on their shoulders. Equal participation therefore does not require identical equipment. The repeated tribal offerings separately give each leader a visible place in the dedication.

passages.title: Levites prepared for service
passages.summary: Aaron tends the lamps. The Levites undergo cleansing and appointment before beginning their service.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how preparation and support can help people serve at different stages of life.

contextNote.title: Ending one duty does not end every form of service
contextNote.text: The instructions distinguish active work from assistance after the stated retirement age. An older Levite can remain involved without carrying the same assignment. The preparation ceremony also connects workers with the larger congregation. Service requires defined limits as well as willingness to contribute.

passages.title: Passover and the guiding cloud
passages.summary: Israel keeps Passover at Sinai. People unable to observe it at the first time receive another date. The cloud directs camp movements.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how faithful observance can include people whose circumstances require accommodation.

contextNote.title: A question from excluded people produces another opportunity
contextNote.text: People unable to keep Passover ask why they should lose participation. Moses brings their concrete case before God. The response supplies a later date rather than ignoring their ritual condition. The law develops through hearing people whose circumstances do not fit the first instruction.

passages.title: Departure from Sinai
passages.summary: God gives instructions for silver trumpets. Israel leaves Sinai. Moses invites Hobab to help guide the journey.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how shared signals and practical experience can help a group act together.

contextNote.title: Divine guidance does not make human knowledge useless
contextNote.text: Moses asks Hobab to help because he knows places to camp. The request appears beside the ark, cloud, and travel signals. These forms of guidance serve different practical needs within the same journey. The account can value local knowledge without replacing its account of God's direction.

passages.title: Complaints, elders, and quail
passages.summary: The people complain about food. Moses asks for help. Seventy elders receive the Spirit, including Eldad and Medad in the camp.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies gratitude and meekness here. Consider Moses’s response to Eldad and Medad.

contextNote.title: Memory changes under pressure
contextNote.text: The people remember Egypt’s food while facing hunger and strain. Their speech leaves forced work out of that memory. The contrast shows how need can change a story about the past. Moses also reaches the limit of his strength. Leadership needs shared help, not only a stronger leader.

passages.title: Miriam and Aaron challenge Moses
passages.summary: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses. God defends Moses’s special role. Miriam becomes afflicted, and Moses prays for her.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies respect for prophetic service. Read that theme alongside Moses’s prayer for Miriam.

contextNote.title: The community's movement waits for an excluded member
contextNote.text: The conflict concerns Moses' authority and his siblings' challenge to it. Miriam's exclusion then stops the camp from moving for seven days. Her condition has consequences beyond an individual punishment. Moses' prayer and the community's waiting also preserve concern within the account of judgment.

passages.title: The spies report on Canaan
passages.summary: Moses sends twelve men to inspect Canaan. They return with fruit and reports of strong settlements. Caleb urges action.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies Caleb's faith. How does fear affect the way people answer the report?

contextNote.title: Observation and conclusion are different parts of the report
contextNote.text: The scouts bring fruit and describe strong settlements. Caleb draws a different conclusion from others who inspected the same land. Their disagreement concerns what the evidence means for action. The chapter lets fear shape interpretation without pretending the reported obstacles are imaginary.

passages.title: The people refuse to enter
passages.summary: The people want to return to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb urge trust. Moses intercedes, and the generation receives a judgment of wandering.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects this account with hope through faith. Consider the duties that accompany trust.

contextNote.title: A later act does not undo the earlier refusal
contextNote.text: The people first refuse to enter when told to go. They later attack after receiving a warning to remain. Their reversal changes direction without restoring obedient timing. The failed advance shows that urgency alone cannot repair the consequences of a community decision.

passages.title: Offerings and reminders
passages.summary: The laws describe offerings after entry into the land. They address unintentional error, deliberate defiance, a Sabbath case, and garment fringes.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How can a visible reminder help someone remember a promise?

contextNote.title: A garment reminder reaches into ordinary acts of looking
contextNote.text: The fringes give the people a visible prompt beyond public ceremonies. The instruction connects seeing with remembering commands and resisting competing desires. It follows laws about error and deliberate defiance. Memory becomes a daily practice within a community that has repeatedly failed to act together.

passages.title: Korah, Dathan, and Abiram rebel
passages.summary: Korah and other leaders challenge Moses and Aaron. The account describes severe judgment and a later plague. Aaron makes atonement for the people.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The manual studies priestly authority. Read the entire account, including the leaders’ concern for people facing judgment.

contextNote.title: A claim about shared holiness challenges unequal duties
contextNote.text: Korah's complaint uses the holiness of the whole congregation against Moses and Aaron. The account nevertheless distinguishes common belonging from assigned service. The later plague also draws Moses and Aaron into protecting their accusers. Disputed authority becomes a crisis over both roles and the community's survival.

passages.title: Aaron’s staff buds
passages.summary: Each tribal leader supplies a staff. Aaron’s staff produces buds, flowers, and almonds. It remains as a sign at the sanctuary.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How does Aaron's flowering staff answer the dispute about leadership?

contextNote.title: A retained sign answers a conflict that speech has not settled
contextNote.text: Each leader's staff gives the test a common starting point. Aaron's living staff then marks a difference among otherwise ordinary objects. Keeping it near the testimony preserves a reminder beyond the event. The sign addresses repeated disputes over service rather than proving every future leader's decision correct.

passages.title: Priestly duties and support
passages.summary: God assigns duties to Aaron, his sons, and the Levites. Offerings and tithes support their service.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider the responsibilities that accompany community support for religious service.

contextNote.title: Support for sanctuary workers creates a duty for its recipients
contextNote.text: The Levites receive tithes because their assigned service replaces a territorial inheritance. They must also give a portion from what they receive. Provision therefore carries obligations rather than becoming unrestricted private wealth. The chapter ties resources, work, and limits to a common sacred center.

passages.title: The red heifer and cleansing
passages.summary: Eleazar oversees the burning of a red cow. Its ashes enter water used after contact with the dead.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What care do people need after a death? How do these rules affect the whole camp?

contextNote.title: Contact with death changes access even without deliberate wrongdoing
contextNote.text: The rules attach a cleansing period to touching a dead body. Such contact can arise from ordinary family and community duties. The procedure distinguishes ritual status from accusations of personal evil. Death creates a problem for access to sacred space within this system.

passages.title: Miriam dies, water flows, and Aaron dies
passages.summary: Miriam dies at Kadesh. Moses strikes the rock during a dispute over water. Edom refuses passage. Aaron dies after Eleazar receives his garments.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Moses's choices under pressure. What help do people need during grief?

contextNote.title: A long-serving leader remains subject to judgment
contextNote.text: Moses and Aaron receive a restriction concerning entry into the land. Their earlier service does not exempt them from the account's stated duty. The chapter also records deaths and the transfer of priestly garments. The journey continues through loss without making any leader indispensable to its completion.

passages.title: The bronze serpent and eastern victories
passages.summary: The people suffer snakebites and receive a bronze serpent as a sign for healing. Israel then defeats Sihon and Og.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the serpent with looking to Christ. Compare Alma 33 and Helaman 8.

contextNote.title: The healing sign later becomes a question about its use
contextNote.text: The bronze serpent gives bitten people a commanded act of looking. The object serves a specific crisis within this chapter. Second Kings 18 later describes destroying it after people burn incense to it. The later account distinguishes a remembered means of rescue from continuing worship of the object.

passages.title: Balak sends for Balaam
passages.summary: Balak asks Balaam to curse Israel. During Balaam’s journey, his donkey sees an angel before he does. Balaam must speak the words God gives.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies how Balaam responds to pressure from the king.

contextNote.title: An outsider sees what a seer misses
contextNote.text: Balaam receives payment offers because others value his power to speak. Yet his donkey sees danger before he does. The reversal questions his control over knowledge. His later words remain subject to God’s command. The story separates paid influence from authority to bless.

passages.title: Balaam blesses Israel
passages.summary: Balak builds altars and seeks a curse. Balaam instead pronounces blessings. They move to another vantage point, but the result remains a blessing.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider the pressure to give an answer that a powerful person wants to hear.

contextNote.title: Changing the viewpoint cannot purchase a different answer
contextNote.text: Balak moves Balaam after receiving an unwanted blessing. The new location changes what Balaam sees but not what he must say. Repeated sacrifices cannot give the king ownership of the message. The scene separates royal resources from authority to determine a divine answer.

passages.title: A star and a scepter
passages.summary: Balaam gives further oracles about Israel and neighboring peoples. Balak dismisses him after the blessings continue.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the star and scepter with Christ.

contextNote.title: A promised reward loses force when the message stays independent
contextNote.text: Balak treats the blessing as a failure that costs Balaam honor. Balaam answers that payment cannot change the words he receives. The poems then extend attention beyond the immediate camp and king. Their images of future rule require interpretation rather than a map of present movements.

passages.title: Peor and Phinehas
passages.summary: Israel joins worship at Peor. Phinehas kills Zimri and Cozbi during the crisis. The account describes the end of a plague.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What responsibilities do people have toward others during a crisis?

contextNote.title: A promise of peace follows a disturbing act of killing
contextNote.text: The account credits Phinehas with ending the crisis through lethal action. It then links his household with a covenant of peace and priestly service. That sequence joins religious approval with deaths the reader must still recognize. The promise concerns Phinehas's line, not a general rule for every act of violence.

passages.title: The second census
passages.summary: Moses and Eleazar count the next generation. The families receive lists, and inheritance depends on group size. Joshua and Caleb survive from the earlier census.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how continuity and change affect a community preparing for a new stage.

contextNote.title: The new count organizes shares for the coming generation
contextNote.text: The census follows the loss of the generation that first left Egypt. Group size now helps determine the amount of land assigned. The count therefore serves a future distribution as well as military readiness. The surviving names of Joshua and Caleb make the break between generations visible.

passages.title: The daughters’ petition and Joshua’s appointment
passages.summary: Zelophehad’s daughters ask for an inheritance because their father had no sons. God accepts their claim. Moses appoints Joshua before the congregation.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how careful listening can reveal a gap in existing rules. The manual also studies Joshua’s appointment.

contextNote.title: A family’s case changes the rule
contextNote.text: The daughters name a gap in the inheritance rules. Without sons, their father’s household could lose its place. Their request leads to a wider rule for other families. Law here includes hearing a concrete case. Read the women’s speech as part of the decision, not a side event.

passages.title: Daily, Sabbath, and festival offerings
passages.summary: God gives offerings for daily worship and special days. These include Sabbaths, new moons, Passover, and the first harvest.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how repeated acts can sustain remembrance and gratitude.

contextNote.title: A calendar creates a recurring claim on shared resources
contextNote.text: The instructions assign offerings to days, weeks, months, and festivals. These gifts require animals, grain, oil, and drink on repeated occasions. Worship therefore depends on planning and provision across time. The coming settlement must sustain a common practice rather than only celebrate one successful arrival.

passages.title: Offerings in the seventh month
passages.summary: God gives offerings for three yearly holy days. These include the trumpet day, the Day of Atonement, and the feast of booths.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how a calendar can help a community remember its duties together.

contextNote.title: The festival's pattern gives time an ordered shape
contextNote.text: The offerings change across the days of the festival rather than remaining identical. The final gathering also limits ordinary work. Numbers, materials, and rest together distinguish this period from daily time. The instructions make celebration an ordered shared duty, not an undefined season of extra activity.

passages.title: Vows and household authority
passages.summary: The laws regulate vows. Fathers and husbands can cancel certain vows made by women under the stated conditions.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Who can cancel a vow in these laws? How does that power affect family members?

contextNote.title: Silence can confirm a vow within an unequal household system
contextNote.text: Fathers and husbands receive power to cancel certain women's vows. The rule also limits when they can act against a promise they have heard. Silence can leave the obligation standing. These timing rules restrain that authority without removing the unequal power given to household members.

passages.title: War against Midian
passages.summary: Israel attacks Midian, and Balaam dies. Moses gives severe instructions about captives. The chapter also divides spoils and describes cleansing.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How does war affect the families in this chapter?

contextNote.title: Victory does not end the account's violence
contextNote.text: The returning army has taken captives as well as goods. Moses orders further deaths among those captives. Later cleansing and distribution organize the aftermath but do not erase those orders. Read the later procedures beside the human cost that a victory summary would hide.

passages.title: Eastern tribes make a promise
passages.summary: Reuben and Gad request land east of the Jordan. Moses requires their fighting men to assist the other tribes. Families can remain in the eastern settlements.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how a personal or group benefit can carry obligations to the wider community.

contextNote.title: A desirable local settlement creates a question of shared burden
contextNote.text: Reuben and Gad see suitable pasture east of the Jordan. Moses asks whether their brothers must fight while they remain behind. Their pledge answers the danger of benefiting without sharing the work. Separate homes become acceptable only within an agreement about common responsibility.

passages.title: The journey remembered
passages.summary: The chapter lists camps from Egypt to the plains of Moab. It then gives instructions for entry into Canaan.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Why might a community keep a list of the places along its journey?

contextNote.title: A journey list turns movement into shared memory
contextNote.text: The stages arrange years of travel through named departures and camps. Not every entry carries a separate story in the book. The list preserves an ordered account even where locations remain uncertain today. Remembering a named stage does not by itself establish its modern coordinates.

passages.title: Borders and appointed leaders
passages.summary: God describes the land’s boundaries and names leaders to divide it. Eleazar and Joshua receive leading roles.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What helps people share land fairly? What duties do the named leaders receive?

contextNote.title: Dividing promised land requires named people to make decisions
contextNote.text: The boundary description sets out the territory before households receive their shares. Named tribal representatives then join Eleazar and Joshua in assigning it. The promise therefore leads into an organized process with human responsibilities. Describing a boundary in the account does not prove control of every place within it.

passages.title: Levite towns and cities of refuge
passages.summary: The law provides towns for Levites and refuge for people accused of killing. It distinguishes accidental death from intentional murder.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how fair judgment requires more than an accusation. Read the ancient procedures within their legal setting.

contextNote.title: Refuge delays revenge so a case can receive judgment
contextNote.text: The cities provide safety before the congregation decides what happened. The law distinguishes intentional killing from death caused without intent. Witnesses and circumstances matter within that distinction. Protection for the accused also serves the community by interrupting immediate private retaliation.

passages.title: Inheritance and marriage
passages.summary: Leaders from Manasseh question the effects of the daughters’ inheritance. The daughters marry within their father’s tribe under the new instruction.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How do the inheritance rules affect Zelophehad's daughters and their choices?

contextNote.title: Protecting an inheritance narrows the daughters' marriage choices
contextNote.text: The daughters' earlier petition secured a family share in the land. This chapter asks how marriage could move that share between tribes. The response preserves their property while restricting whom they may marry. A successful claim therefore remains inside a system with other collective interests and limits.

events.title: The first census
events.summary: God commands a census of men eligible for war. Tribal leaders assist Moses and Aaron. Levites receive separate duties.
events.detail: The count focuses on men old enough to serve in war. It therefore does not list every person living in the camp. Tribal leaders organize the count, while Levites receive separate responsibilities. These totals prepare the account for movement and conflict.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How do the camp's different duties help people support each other?

events.title: The camp arranged
events.summary: The tribes camp around the meeting tent in four groups. Their marching order follows the same arrangement.
events.detail: The tribes receive places around the meeting tent rather than independent camps without relation. Their marching order preserves that larger arrangement during movement. The center carries sacred duties instead of belonging to one tribe's army. Space becomes a way to describe both common identity and distinct responsibilities.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider what your daily arrangements show about your priorities.

events.title: Levites and firstborn
events.summary: The chapter names Aaron’s sons and assigns duties to the Levite families. Levites stand in place of Israel’s firstborn.
events.detail: God describes taking the Levites in place of Israel's firstborn sons. This explanation joins present duties with the earlier departure from Egypt. The counting and redemption payments organize that substitution in practical terms. A rescued people carries obligations that reach beyond remembering the rescue in words.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects the firstborn with Israel's escape from Egypt.

events.title: Duties for moving the sanctuary
events.summary: Moses and Aaron count Levites assigned to service. Kohath, Gershon, and Merari have different transport duties.
events.detail: Priests cover the furnishings before others carry them. The carriers must follow limits on touching and seeing the objects. Different families transport different parts of the dwelling. The account makes coordinated work necessary for keeping a sacred center within a traveling camp.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how careful preparation can help others carry their responsibilities.

events.title: Camp, restitution, and jealousy
events.summary: The laws cover camp rules and repayment for wrongs. They include a ceremony for accusations against a wife.
events.detail: The procedure begins with a husband's jealousy, including suspicion without witnesses. It places the accused wife within a public priestly rite. The chapter supplies no matching procedure for a wife suspecting her husband. Its appeal to divine judgment does not erase that unequal starting position.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What power does a husband's accusation give him? What protection does the wife receive?

events.title: Nazirite vows and blessing
events.summary: People can make a special vow to God. It limits wine, hair cutting, and contact with the dead. God also gives priests words of blessing.
events.detail: Women and men can enter the dedication described here. The restrictions govern drink, hair, and contact with death while the vow lasts. An unexpected death nearby requires beginning the dedicated period again. The chapter then moves from individual vows to words blessing the whole people.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how a commitment can shape daily conduct. Read the blessing as a prayer for God’s care.

events.title: Gifts from the tribal leaders
events.summary: Tribal leaders bring wagons, oxen, and offerings for the sanctuary. Each leader’s altar gift receives a separate account.
events.detail: Wagons and oxen go to Levite families according to their transport tasks. The Kohathites receive none because they carry sacred furnishings on their shoulders. Equal participation therefore does not require identical equipment. The repeated tribal offerings separately give each leader a visible place in the dedication.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how material gifts and practical support can make shared worship possible.

events.title: Levites prepared for service
events.summary: Aaron tends the lamps. The Levites undergo cleansing and appointment before beginning their service.
events.detail: The instructions distinguish active work from assistance after the stated retirement age. An older Levite can remain involved without carrying the same assignment. The preparation ceremony also connects workers with the larger congregation. Service requires defined limits as well as willingness to contribute.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how preparation and support can help people serve at different stages of life.

events.title: Passover and the guiding cloud
events.summary: Israel keeps Passover at Sinai. People unable to observe it at the first time receive another date. The cloud directs camp movements.
events.detail: People unable to keep Passover ask why they should lose participation. Moses brings their concrete case before God. The response supplies a later date rather than ignoring their ritual condition. The law develops through hearing people whose circumstances do not fit the first instruction.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how faithful observance can include people whose circumstances require accommodation.

events.title: Departure from Sinai
events.summary: God gives instructions for silver trumpets. Israel leaves Sinai. Moses invites Hobab to help guide the journey.
events.detail: Moses asks Hobab to help because he knows places to camp. The request appears beside the ark, cloud, and travel signals. These forms of guidance serve different practical needs within the same journey. The account can value local knowledge without replacing its account of God's direction.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how shared signals and practical experience can help a group act together.

events.title: Complaints, elders, and quail
events.summary: The people complain about food. Moses asks for help. Seventy elders receive the Spirit, including Eldad and Medad in the camp.
events.detail: The people remember Egypt’s food while facing hunger and strain. Their speech leaves forced work out of that memory. The contrast shows how need can change a story about the past. Moses also reaches the limit of his strength. Leadership needs shared help, not only a stronger leader.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies gratitude and meekness here. Consider Moses’s response to Eldad and Medad.

events.title: Miriam and Aaron challenge Moses
events.summary: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses. God defends Moses’s special role. Miriam becomes afflicted, and Moses prays for her.
events.detail: The conflict concerns Moses' authority and his siblings' challenge to it. Miriam's exclusion then stops the camp from moving for seven days. Her condition has consequences beyond an individual punishment. Moses' prayer and the community's waiting also preserve concern within the account of judgment.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies respect for prophetic service. Read that theme alongside Moses’s prayer for Miriam.

events.title: The spies report on Canaan
events.summary: Moses sends twelve men to inspect Canaan. They return with fruit and reports of strong settlements. Caleb urges action.
events.detail: The scouts bring fruit and describe strong settlements. Caleb draws a different conclusion from others who inspected the same land. Their disagreement concerns what the evidence means for action. The chapter lets fear shape interpretation without pretending the reported obstacles are imaginary.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies Caleb's faith. How does fear affect the way people answer the report?

events.title: The people refuse to enter
events.summary: The people want to return to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb urge trust. Moses intercedes, and the generation receives a judgment of wandering.
events.detail: The people first refuse to enter when told to go. They later attack after receiving a warning to remain. Their reversal changes direction without restoring obedient timing. The failed advance shows that urgency alone cannot repair the consequences of a community decision.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects this account with hope through faith. Consider the duties that accompany trust.

events.title: Offerings and reminders
events.summary: The laws describe offerings after entry into the land. They address unintentional error, deliberate defiance, a Sabbath case, and garment fringes.
events.detail: The fringes give the people a visible prompt beyond public ceremonies. The instruction connects seeing with remembering commands and resisting competing desires. It follows laws about error and deliberate defiance. Memory becomes a daily practice within a community that has repeatedly failed to act together.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How can a visible reminder help someone remember a promise?

events.title: Korah, Dathan, and Abiram rebel
events.summary: Korah and other leaders challenge Moses and Aaron. The account describes severe judgment and a later plague. Aaron makes atonement for the people.
events.detail: Korah's complaint uses the holiness of the whole congregation against Moses and Aaron. The account nevertheless distinguishes common belonging from assigned service. The later plague also draws Moses and Aaron into protecting their accusers. Disputed authority becomes a crisis over both roles and the community's survival.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The manual studies priestly authority. Read the entire account, including the leaders’ concern for people facing judgment.

events.title: Aaron’s staff buds
events.summary: Each tribal leader supplies a staff. Aaron’s staff produces buds, flowers, and almonds. It remains as a sign at the sanctuary.
events.detail: Each leader's staff gives the test a common starting point. Aaron's living staff then marks a difference among otherwise ordinary objects. Keeping it near the testimony preserves a reminder beyond the event. The sign addresses repeated disputes over service rather than proving every future leader's decision correct.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How does Aaron's flowering staff answer the dispute about leadership?

events.title: Priestly duties and support
events.summary: God assigns duties to Aaron, his sons, and the Levites. Offerings and tithes support their service.
events.detail: The Levites receive tithes because their assigned service replaces a territorial inheritance. They must also give a portion from what they receive. Provision therefore carries obligations rather than becoming unrestricted private wealth. The chapter ties resources, work, and limits to a common sacred center.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider the responsibilities that accompany community support for religious service.

events.title: The red heifer and cleansing
events.summary: Eleazar oversees the burning of a red cow. Its ashes enter water used after contact with the dead.
events.detail: The rules attach a cleansing period to touching a dead body. Such contact can arise from ordinary family and community duties. The procedure distinguishes ritual status from accusations of personal evil. Death creates a problem for access to sacred space within this system.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What care do people need after a death? How do these rules affect the whole camp?

events.title: Miriam dies, water flows, and Aaron dies
events.summary: Miriam dies at Kadesh. Moses strikes the rock during a dispute over water. Edom refuses passage. Aaron dies after Eleazar receives his garments.
events.detail: Moses and Aaron receive a restriction concerning entry into the land. Their earlier service does not exempt them from the account's stated duty. The chapter also records deaths and the transfer of priestly garments. The journey continues through loss without making any leader indispensable to its completion.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Moses's choices under pressure. What help do people need during grief?

events.title: The bronze serpent and eastern victories
events.summary: The people suffer snakebites and receive a bronze serpent as a sign for healing. Israel then defeats Sihon and Og.
events.detail: The bronze serpent gives bitten people a commanded act of looking. The object serves a specific crisis within this chapter. Second Kings 18 later describes destroying it after people burn incense to it. The later account distinguishes a remembered means of rescue from continuing worship of the object.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the serpent with looking to Christ. Compare Alma 33 and Helaman 8.

events.title: Balak sends for Balaam
events.summary: Balak asks Balaam to curse Israel. During Balaam’s journey, his donkey sees an angel before he does. Balaam must speak the words God gives.
events.detail: Balaam receives payment offers because others value his power to speak. Yet his donkey sees danger before he does. The reversal questions his control over knowledge. His later words remain subject to God’s command. The story separates paid influence from authority to bless.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies how Balaam responds to pressure from the king.

events.title: Balaam blesses Israel
events.summary: Balak builds altars and seeks a curse. Balaam instead pronounces blessings. They move to another vantage point, but the result remains a blessing.
events.detail: Balak moves Balaam after receiving an unwanted blessing. The new location changes what Balaam sees but not what he must say. Repeated sacrifices cannot give the king ownership of the message. The scene separates royal resources from authority to determine a divine answer.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider the pressure to give an answer that a powerful person wants to hear.

events.title: A star and a scepter
events.summary: Balaam gives further oracles about Israel and neighboring peoples. Balak dismisses him after the blessings continue.
events.detail: Balak treats the blessing as a failure that costs Balaam honor. Balaam answers that payment cannot change the words he receives. The poems then extend attention beyond the immediate camp and king. Their images of future rule require interpretation rather than a map of present movements.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the star and scepter with Christ.

events.title: Peor and Phinehas
events.summary: Israel joins worship at Peor. Phinehas kills Zimri and Cozbi during the crisis. The account describes the end of a plague.
events.detail: The account credits Phinehas with ending the crisis through lethal action. It then links his household with a covenant of peace and priestly service. That sequence joins religious approval with deaths the reader must still recognize. The promise concerns Phinehas's line, not a general rule for every act of violence.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What responsibilities do people have toward others during a crisis?

events.title: The second census
events.summary: Moses and Eleazar count the next generation. The families receive lists, and inheritance depends on group size. Joshua and Caleb survive from the earlier census.
events.detail: The census follows the loss of the generation that first left Egypt. Group size now helps determine the amount of land assigned. The count therefore serves a future distribution as well as military readiness. The surviving names of Joshua and Caleb make the break between generations visible.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how continuity and change affect a community preparing for a new stage.

events.title: The daughters’ petition and Joshua’s appointment
events.summary: Zelophehad’s daughters ask for an inheritance because their father had no sons. God accepts their claim. Moses appoints Joshua before the congregation.
events.detail: The daughters name a gap in the inheritance rules. Without sons, their father’s household could lose its place. Their request leads to a wider rule for other families. Law here includes hearing a concrete case. Read the women’s speech as part of the decision, not a side event.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how careful listening can reveal a gap in existing rules. The manual also studies Joshua’s appointment.

events.title: Daily, Sabbath, and festival offerings
events.summary: God gives offerings for daily worship and special days. These include Sabbaths, new moons, Passover, and the first harvest.
events.detail: The instructions assign offerings to days, weeks, months, and festivals. These gifts require animals, grain, oil, and drink on repeated occasions. Worship therefore depends on planning and provision across time. The coming settlement must sustain a common practice rather than only celebrate one successful arrival.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how repeated acts can sustain remembrance and gratitude.

events.title: Offerings in the seventh month
events.summary: God gives offerings for three yearly holy days. These include the trumpet day, the Day of Atonement, and the feast of booths.
events.detail: The offerings change across the days of the festival rather than remaining identical. The final gathering also limits ordinary work. Numbers, materials, and rest together distinguish this period from daily time. The instructions make celebration an ordered shared duty, not an undefined season of extra activity.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how a calendar can help a community remember its duties together.

events.title: Vows and household authority
events.summary: The laws regulate vows. Fathers and husbands can cancel certain vows made by women under the stated conditions.
events.detail: Fathers and husbands receive power to cancel certain women's vows. The rule also limits when they can act against a promise they have heard. Silence can leave the obligation standing. These timing rules restrain that authority without removing the unequal power given to household members.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Who can cancel a vow in these laws? How does that power affect family members?

events.title: War against Midian
events.summary: Israel attacks Midian, and Balaam dies. Moses gives severe instructions about captives. The chapter also divides spoils and describes cleansing.
events.detail: The returning army has taken captives as well as goods. Moses orders further deaths among those captives. Later cleansing and distribution organize the aftermath but do not erase those orders. Read the later procedures beside the human cost that a victory summary would hide.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How does war affect the families in this chapter?

events.title: Eastern tribes make a promise
events.summary: Reuben and Gad request land east of the Jordan. Moses requires their fighting men to assist the other tribes. Families can remain in the eastern settlements.
events.detail: Reuben and Gad see suitable pasture east of the Jordan. Moses asks whether their brothers must fight while they remain behind. Their pledge answers the danger of benefiting without sharing the work. Separate homes become acceptable only within an agreement about common responsibility.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how a personal or group benefit can carry obligations to the wider community.

events.title: The journey remembered
events.summary: The chapter lists camps from Egypt to the plains of Moab. It then gives instructions for entry into Canaan.
events.detail: The stages arrange years of travel through named departures and camps. Not every entry carries a separate story in the book. The list preserves an ordered account even where locations remain uncertain today. Remembering a named stage does not by itself establish its modern coordinates.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Why might a community keep a list of the places along its journey?

events.title: Borders and appointed leaders
events.summary: God describes the land’s boundaries and names leaders to divide it. Eleazar and Joshua receive leading roles.
events.detail: The boundary description sets out the territory before households receive their shares. Named tribal representatives then join Eleazar and Joshua in assigning it. The promise therefore leads into an organized process with human responsibilities. Describing a boundary in the account does not prove control of every place within it.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What helps people share land fairly? What duties do the named leaders receive?

events.title: Levite towns and cities of refuge
events.summary: The law provides towns for Levites and refuge for people accused of killing. It distinguishes accidental death from intentional murder.
events.detail: The cities provide safety before the congregation decides what happened. The law distinguishes intentional killing from death caused without intent. Witnesses and circumstances matter within that distinction. Protection for the accused also serves the community by interrupting immediate private retaliation.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how fair judgment requires more than an accusation. Read the ancient procedures within their legal setting.

events.title: Inheritance and marriage
events.summary: Leaders from Manasseh question the effects of the daughters’ inheritance. The daughters marry within their father’s tribe under the new instruction.
events.detail: The daughters' earlier petition secured a family share in the land. This chapter asks how marriage could move that share between tribes. The response preserves their property while restricting whom they may marry. A successful claim therefore remains inside a system with other collective interests and limits.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Memory changes under pressure
steps.text: The people remember Egypt’s food while facing hunger and strain. Their speech leaves forced work out of that memory. The contrast shows how need can change a story about the past. Moses also reaches the limit of his strength. Leadership needs shared help, not only a stronger leader.

steps.title: An outsider sees what a seer misses
steps.text: Balaam receives payment offers because others value his power to speak. Yet his donkey sees danger before he does. The reversal questions his control over knowledge. His later words remain subject to God’s command. The story separates paid influence from authority to bless.

steps.text: The daughters name a gap in the inheritance rules. Without sons, their father’s household could lose its place. Their request leads to a wider rule for other families. Law here includes hearing a concrete case. Read the women’s speech as part of the decision, not a side event.

textRoutes.title: The journey remembered
textRoutes.summary: The chapter lists camps from Egypt to the plains of Moab. It then gives instructions for entry into Canaan.
textRoutes.detail: The stages arrange years of travel through named departures and camps. Not every entry carries a separate story in the book. The list preserves an ordered account even where locations remain uncertain today. Remembering a named stage does not by itself establish its modern coordinates.
textRoutes.uncertainty: Numbers 33 names this broad sequence. The line omits uncertain camps and does not show an excavated travel path.
